problems.statement: A silent, unnotified routing rule (RR-17) put all SlotBook tickets in an unsupported best-effort P4 queue with no target. Arts was never told: the change record had no external notification, no ITS-Arts email trail exists, and the auto-acknowledgement hides the status. This is the main cause of Arts' long waits and of the dispute.
Central IT is generally unresponsive to Arts (the Dean's framing); Arts' non-SlotBook tickets match comparable non-Arts tickets within 0.3 days, so there is no general ITS bias against Arts.

Lindqvist campus on-site coverage (a technician only on Tuesdays and Thursdays) causes slow on-site hardware tickets for Arts and Education. Arts has a higher on-site share (31% vs 14%), and arrival takes 4.7 business days against 0.6 on the main campus. This is a real second, location-based gap that the Dean's story and ITS's blame of Arts both miss.

Arts staff raise excessive trivial or duplicate tickets, as the ITS Director claims. Duplicate and how-to shares are at or below the university rate. The excess ticket volume comes from SlotBook, which is unsupported and itself generates ticket churn from repeated unanswered tickets.

SlotBook is an unsupported, undocumented, fragile legacy app with no owner (PHP 5.6, built by a departed postdoc). Six departments depend on it for about 1,900 sections a term, and CampusBook cannot do its repeating multi-section patterns. It is a latent operational and security risk that nobody owns, and the ITS claim that CampusBook covers everything is unverified.

The ITS Director told the then Arts Operations Manager about RR-17 on 2025-08-12 (so Arts 'knew'). The only evidence is the Director's own account and a calendar entry. There is no agenda, email or notes, the manager retired and declined to be interviewed, and the Dean and the successor were never told. Whether Arts was informed cannot be settled, and even if it was, the knowledge never reached anyone who could act.

The SlotBook ticket surge in September 2025 was caused by the SSO migration of 2025-09-08. SlotBook reportedly uses local passwords, the term-start peak is a confounder, and earlier counts are undercounted. The History administrator's report of flaky logins since the login change conflicts with this. Server logs are not accessible.

Philosophy's email-migration delay shows ITS is 'hopeless across the board'. The ticket spent 11 of 15 days waiting on the requester, with first response in 0.4 days and under 1 day of active ITS time. The perception is a measurement and communication artefact, and the survey's general dissatisfaction is mostly tied to SlotBook and timetabling.

ITS service desk capacity is strained (21 FTE, cut from 23, 94% utilisation) but is not the cause of Arts' delay. P2 and P3 queues met targets in 10 of 12 months, and the best-effort queue is staffed at only 0.4 FTE.

causalClaims.from: RR-17 routing SlotBook tickets to P4 with no target
causalClaims.to: SlotBook median resolution of 21 days (17 days before first technician action)
Arts' overall median resolution gap versus the university (about 70% of the gap)

causalClaims.from: No external notification of RR-17 plus the generic ACK-P4 acknowledgement
causalClaims.to: Arts staff and leadership being unaware of the best-effort status, and the perception of unresponsiveness

causalClaims.from: Lindqvist campus on-site technician cover of two days a week
causalClaims.to: slower on-site hardware resolution for Arts and Education

causalClaims.from: Arts staff behaviour (trivial or duplicate tickets)
The RR-17 category and the surge in SlotBook tickets

causalClaims.to: unanswered, repeated tickets that inflate Arts ticket volume

actions.action: Do not approve transferring 2 FTE of service desk budget to an Arts-run desk. The diagnosis does not support a separate desk, which would not fix SlotBook (unsupported by anyone) or the Lindqvist on-site cover gap, and would take capacity from a desk running at 94% utilisation.
actions.rationale: The Dean's proposal answers a diagnosis the evidence rejects (general ITS unresponsiveness).

actions.action: Adopt ITS's proposal to put all Arts tickets on best-effort. Non-SlotBook Arts tickets perform like everyone else's, so this would penalise about 2,260 supported tickets a year and turn a narrow problem into a real one.
actions.rationale: It is contradicted by the like-for-like comparison and punishes the wrong thing.

actions.action: Fix the notification and acknowledgement gap now. Change ACK-P4 to state best-effort status and give an expected time, formally tell the Dean and the current Operations Manager about RR-17, and require external notification in the change record.
actions.rationale: This is cheap, removes the hidden-rule cause of the dispute, and works whatever the August 2025 meeting contained.

actions.action: Give SlotBook an interim arrangement. Triage SlotBook tickets by impact (timetable clashes affect teaching), set a basic target or a named contact, and put an ITS and Arts owner on the server and its risk.
actions.rationale: Six departments run about 1,900 sections a term on an unowned PHP 5.6 system, and a 21-day median is unacceptable, while a fix does not depend on the SSO question.

actions.action: Do a joint requirements-fit assessment of SlotBook against CampusBook (including repeating multi-section patterns) before the January 2027 move, and scope and cost a migration or a supported-service decision.
actions.rationale: Neither the ITS claim that CampusBook covers everything nor the Arts claim that it cannot is verified, and no assessment exists.

actions.action: Address Lindqvist on-site coverage, for example more technician days or remote or locker swap options, with Education as a co-sponsor.
actions.rationale: Arrival takes 4.7 days against 0.6, and this is a real, separate, measurable disparity that is not Arts' fault.

actions.action: Retire SlotBook by force for January 2027 with no fit assessment.
actions.rationale: It risks disrupting teaching timetabling if CampusBook cannot handle the patterns.

actions.action: Spend effort on a blame finding about whether Arts was told in August 2025.
actions.rationale: The record cannot settle it, and the fixes do not depend on it.

actions.action: Set up per-queue reporting that separates awaiting-requester time from active time, and share it with Arts.
actions.rationale: The measurement artefact (as in the Philosophy ticket) inflates perceived delay and lets each side tell a different story.

nextEvidence: A requirements-fit comparison of SlotBook and CampusBook, especially repeating multi-section patterns, with the cost and risk of keeping SlotBook as it is
SlotBook server and login logs, or a test, showing whether the 2025-09-08 SSO migration affected logins, and the monthly count of repeat or follow-up SlotBook tickets

The impact of SlotBook delays on teaching, such as the number of room clashes per term and the sections affected, plus any record of what the 2025-08-12 meeting covered (for example from the former manager)
output.summary: The Dean's account is mostly wrong, and so is ITS's. Arts is not generally neglected: its non-SlotBook tickets resolve like everyone else's. The main cause is RR-17, a routing rule that sent every SlotBook ticket to an unstaffed, target-free best-effort queue (median 21 days). It was never formally communicated, and the generic acknowledgement hid it. That accounts for about 70% of the gap. A separate, real cause is the Lindqvist campus having technician cover only two days a week. SlotBook itself is an unowned, fragile legacy system. Recommend notification fixes, SlotBook triage, a fit assessment and Lindqvist cover. Do not fund an Arts desk or put all Arts tickets on best-effort.
